verdicts.text: SST (Serverless Stack) originally used AWS CDK as a starting point for its infrastructure tooling.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own v2 repo (sst/v2, packages/sst/package.json) lists CDK as core dependencies: "aws-cdk-lib": "2.224.0", "constructs": "10.3.0", "cdk-assets", "@aws-cdk/toolkit-lib". The current SST (v3) is a separate codebase. That confirms the earlier SST was built on AWS CDK.
verdicts.framing_note: Checked against SST's own source code, not the blog post. The claim's "originally" (i.e., "first") is inferred from the v2→v3 split; the repo doesn't state it directly.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's AWS CDK comparison page backs this up: "AWS CDK transpiles programs into AWS CloudFormation templates that the AWS CloudFormation service deploys, and supports AWS only" and "CDK is AWS-only." That page is on Pulumi's own site, so it supports the claim but can't prove it alone. The claim also fits how CDK is widely known to work: it deploys only through CloudFormation. Line 64 says it in the past tense ("CDK tied infrastructure to AWS"), as part of SST's story.
verdicts.framing_note: Only other Pulumi pages back this up. The CDK constructs library is also used by other tools (CDKTF, cdk8s), but AWS CDK itself only deploys to AWS through CloudFormation.

verdicts.text: Debugging SST's CDK-based infrastructure was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own post announcing the move away from CDK describes CloudFormation as opaque and says CDK "will generate JSON CloudFormation templates that won't work". It also says issues in the CDK/CFN model "can be really hard to debug", which supports the claim's gist. SST never uses the word "frustrating" itself; that part is the blog's own wording.
verdicts.framing_note: SST source: "we are not dealing with the CloudFormation black box" (about Ion) and "This can be really hard to debug". The claim's "frustrating due to CloudFormation templates" is a fair paraphrase.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible for SST when built on AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Independent sources confirm the substance: AWS CDK only targets AWS, and SST v2 was tied to it. fireup.pro says "CDK also locked SST into the AWS ecosystem," and Encore says "CDK is AWS only." SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post confirms Ion replaced CDK/CloudFormation with Pulumi and Terraform providers. "Nearly impossible" is the blog's own wording, not a quote from SST.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "locked SST into the AWS ecosystem"; the claim says "nearly impossible." This is the blog's own characterization, and it fits the sources.

verdicts.text: SST was originally built on top of AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own blog confirms SST v2 was built on CDK: "At the end of the day, SST v2 is open source and built on CDK." AWS CDK itself supports TypeScript and Python, among other languages, so the sentence is accurate if "which" refers to CDK.
verdicts.framing_note: The "TypeScript or Python" clause describes CDK. It is misleading if read as describing SST, because SST's constructs and config were TypeScript/JavaScript only.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Readers may think SST v2 let you define infrastructure in Python. As far as I know it didn't; Python was only a Lambda runtime. Consider rewording to "TypeScript" or making clear the clause is about CDK.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: This is accurate. Pulumi's CDK comparison page says CDK is "for defining AWS infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, and Java", and its comparison table lists "TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, C#, and Java". So TypeScript and Python are supported, but the claim lists only two of CDK's six languages.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "TypeScript or Python" leaves out JavaScript, Go, C#, and Java. It's true as written, but readers could take it as the full list; consider "e.g." or naming all six languages.

verdicts.text: With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) which is then executed to deploy resources.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi CDK comparison page, which quotes AWS's own Cloud Assembly docs, says: "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." That backs up the claim that CDK code generates YAML/JSON, which CloudFormation then deploys.
verdicts.framing_note: The inline link goes to a general 'What is AWS CloudFormation' section, not to a source for this specific claim. Also, "code generator" really describes CDK; with plain CloudFormation, people write the YAML/JSON templates by hand.

verdicts.text: With CDK and CloudFormation, the code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during the deployment process.
verdicts.evidence: This matches how CDK is built: CDK is a transpiler. The Pulumi comparison page says "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." So the CloudFormation templates that get deployed are not the program the developer wrote. I found no problem with the claim; it's an accurate, somewhat loose description of how CDK synthesis works.
verdicts.framing_note: This is general architecture, and the blog attributes it to the SST team's experience. The corroborating source is a Pulumi editorial page rather than AWS docs, so confidence is medium, not high.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK has an AWS-centric nature that limits its use outside the AWS ecosystem.
verdicts.evidence: The page the claim links to (the Pulumi AWS CDK comparison) says: "CDK is AWS-only" and that CDK "transpiles programs into AWS CloudFormation templates that the AWS CloudFormation service deploys, and supports AWS only." This fits how CDK is widely known to work: it synthesizes to CloudFormation, and third-party resources come in only through CloudFormation Registry extensions or Lambda-backed custom resources.
verdicts.framing_note: The linked page says CDK "supports AWS only"; the blog says its "AWS-centric nature" limits use outside AWS. Both make the same point. The blog frames it as the SST team's experience.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The only corroboration comes from Pulumi's own site, which is not neutral. CDK for Terraform (CDKTF) is a separate project that does support multiple clouds, but it is not AWS CDK.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi publishes first-party providers for AWS (pulumi-aws), Azure (pulumi-azure-native), and GCP (pulumi-gcp), plus on-premises providers such as pulumi-vsphere: "A Pulumi resource package for VMWare VSphere, providing multi-language access to vCenter Server and ESXi".

verdicts.text: AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: L102 is a comparison-table cell ("❌ Hard due to CloudFormation"). It gives a subjective opinion based on SST's experience, which the post explains at L95 ("This can lead to several problems, such as difficulty debugging"). "Hard" is a judgment no source can prove true or false. The fact underneath it, that CDK synthesizes CloudFormation templates which then get deployed, is well known and matches the post's description.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a marketing comparison table; other rows (e.g., 'TypeScript, Python' for CDK language support, 'AWS Secrets Manager only') may be more checkable and possibly inaccurate.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides real-time debugging.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated `pulumi up` CLI reference lists "--attach-debugger ... Enable the ability to attach a debugger to the program and source based plugins being executed". So you can attach a debugger to a running Pulumi program, which reasonably supports "real-time debugging". The claim sits in a comparison-table cell and uses loose marketing wording, not a specific product feature name.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Real-time debugging" is vague marketing wording. Pulumi's actual feature is attaching a live debugger (--attach-debugger) plus verbose --debug output, so reviewers may want more specific wording.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as languages.
verdicts.evidence: The aws/aws-cdk README (fetched as base64 and decoded) says: "The CDK is available in the following languages: * JavaScript, TypeScript ... * Python ... * Java ... * .NET ... * Go". So CDK is not limited to TypeScript and Python. The repo's own CDK comparison page agrees, listing "TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, C#, and Java".
verdicts.framing_note: Table row L103 lists CDK language support as only "TypeScript, Python". L87 frames the same two languages as SST's historical usage, which is fine, but the comparison table presents them as CDK's full language support.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports any programming language.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi supports a fixed set of languages, not "any". The languages overview says: "Pulumi supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL," and adds: "If your favorite language isn't listed... it's possible to add your own language." The core repo backs this up: its sdk/ directory ships only go, nodejs and python, while .NET, Java, YAML and HCL are separate repos.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is L103, the Pulumi cell of the "Language Support" row in the comparison table. The same post's CTA (L159) lists only "TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#", so the page contradicts itself. Suggested fix: list the supported languages instead.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any programming language" is an absolute that no IaC tool can meet. The CDK cell in the same row ("TypeScript, Python") is also too narrow: CDK also supports Java, C#, Go and JavaScript.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK supports secrets management only through AWS Secrets Manager.
verdicts.evidence: The AWS CDK source docstring for SecretValue says secrets should be stored "in an external system like AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, and you can reference them by calling `SecretValue.secretsManager()` or `SecretValue.ssmSecure()`". The same class also offers `cfnParameter` (NoEcho parameters) and `cfnDynamicReference`, so Secrets Manager isn't the only option.
verdicts.framing_note: Comparison-table cell at L108: "❌ AWS Secrets Manager only". A fairer version would be "AWS-native secret stores only (Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store)".

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides clear deployment state visibility.
verdicts.evidence: This comes from a comparison-table cell ("✅ Clear deployment state"). Pulumi does expose deployment state: the auto-generated CLI reference describes `pulumi stack` as "Manage stacks and view stack state", and says each stack keeps "update history ... in addition to a full checkpoint of the last known good update." Whether that visibility is "clear" is a subjective marketing judgment that no source can confirm.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Subjective comparison-table cell; the underlying capability (state/history visibility) exists, but "clear" is a matter of opinion.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's docs cover custom providers: dynamic providers (TypeScript/Python) and bridged or native providers. The dynamic-providers page says they "are lighter weight than custom providers… For more sophisticated APIs, one can create a bridged or native provider." The claim's "workflows" part is vague, but Automation API and similar tooling support it.

verdicts.text: Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, rather than generating an intermediary format.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide says that during `pulumi up` "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program", and the program then sends resource registrations straight to the engine as it runs. Nothing in that flow produces a template or other intermediate artifact, which fits the claim's contrast with CDK's CloudFormation synthesis.
verdicts.framing_note: Only corroborated by a pulumi.com editorial guide, not product source, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: With Pulumi, the infrastructure code running during deployment is the same code the developer wrote.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) A separate docs page (not the reviewed blog post) describes the runtime this way: "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program... The language host continues to execute your program concurrently with the engine processing this request." In other words, the program the user wrote runs directly during `pulumi up`, and nothing is synthesized into an intermediate template first.
verdicts.framing_note: Backed by an editorial docs page on the same site (corroborating, not product source). The claim loosely paraphrases a documented architectural fact.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allows the SST team to work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi providers docs describe a provider model that covers many clouds, SaaS services, and on-prem devices: "a provider for the cloud, SaaS service, or on-prem device you need" can be used through the Any Terraform Provider, and the providers "let a Pulumi program reach the full breadth of the infrastructure-as-code ecosystem." That backs the general capability claim. The part about SST's own use of it is the blog's story and wasn't checked separately.

verdicts.text: The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) A Pulumi event page confirms that SST had a "Founding Engineer": it lists "Dax Raad (Founding Engineer, SST)" as giving the PulumiUP 2024 talk "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST". But no independent source (a talk transcript, SST blog or interview) had the quoted sentence. The only place it seems to appear is the live copy of the page under review, which can't verify itself.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "\"deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code\" Pulumi"; top results didn't address the claim. Role corroboration: https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/
verdicts.intuition_flag: The quote is credited to a job title rather than a named person (Dax Raad), and the wording reads like marketing copy. Check it against the PulumiUP 2024 talk recording or ask SST to confirm it is verbatim.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities, as described on the Pulumi Insights product page (https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/).
verdicts.evidence: /product/pulumi-insights/ is now an alias of content/product/discovery-governance.md, a page about compliance and resource search. It does mention visibility: "Pulumi discovers all resources... providing complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting." But it says nothing about debugging deployments, which is what the blog sentence is about ("the infrastructure code being the same as the deployment code, they could easily trace issues back to the source").
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the target page says 'complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting' of cloud resources; the claim uses it to support 'improved visibility and debugging' of the deployment process that comes from Pulumi's execution model.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link redirects to the Discovery & governance page, so the 'Pulumi Insights product page' name is out of date. It should point somewhere relevant to debugging, or be relabeled.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi does document built-in extensibility features. The docs cover custom providers and "Dynamic resource providers" (in dynamic-providers.md: "they are lighter weight than custom providers"), and separately component resources. But Pulumi has no feature called "dynamic components": the phrase merges dynamic providers with component resources.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is right that the features exist, but the name is wrong: "dynamic components" should read "dynamic providers" (or "component resources").
verdicts.intuition_flag: "dynamic components" is not a Pulumi term, so it is likely an LLM-style merge of "dynamic providers" and "component resources".

verdicts.text: Pulumi allows defining infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploying it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
verdicts.evidence: The Languages & SDKs docs say: "Pulumi supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL. Each language is equally capable and supports the full surface area of all Pulumi Registry providers." The Registry includes AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud providers, plus on-prem ones like Kubernetes and vSphere. The claim names only four of the supported languages, but it doesn't say those are the only ones.
verdicts.framing_note: The language list is shorter than the full set Pulumi supports, but it's still accurate.

verdicts.text: Pulumi allows deploying infrastructure across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi concepts docs say "Every Pulumi-supported language is equally capable of provisioning and managing infrastructure across all major clouds" and link getting-started guides for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Kubernetes. On-premises coverage comes from Pulumi providers such as pulumi/pulumi-vsphere and Kubernetes, all run through the same CLI workflow.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides improved visibility into the deployment process as described at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The cited page is live, but it now sells cloud asset and compliance management. The "visibility" it describes is about resources and governance, not the deployment process: "Pulumi discovers all resources, including those created outside infrastructure-as-code, providing complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting."
verdicts.source: http://pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights (search snippet, title "Pulumi Insights - Cloud Asset and Compliance Management"); WebSearch ran query "pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights"
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says "complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting" of discovered resources, while the claim says "improved visibility into the deployment process." Only mention is incidental: "immediate policy feedback during deployment."
verdicts.intuition_flag: Deployment-process visibility (update logs, previews, deployment history) is a Pulumi Cloud/Deployments feature, not Insights. The link target may be wrong for this sentence.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides better visibility into the deployment process, as described at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's Insights material talks about visibility into cloud resources and infrastructure, e.g. "comprehensive cloud visibility and policy enforcement—discover all infrastructure and ensure compliance". None of the pages found say anything about visibility into the deployment process, and none compare Pulumi with CDK as "better".
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/ ; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/concepts/ (WebSearch ran query "Pulumi Insights product page"; the cited /product/pulumi-insights/ page itself did not come up in results)
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says "cloud visibility" (resource search/discovery), but the claim says "better visibility into the deployment process". The subject changes and a comparison is added that the source doesn't make.
verdicts.intuition_flag: SST's visibility complaint was probably about opaque CloudFormation deployments. Insights is a resource search/analytics product, so this link may be the wrong citation; update logs or previews in the Pulumi Cloud docs would fit better.

verdicts.text: There is a Pulumi AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/ that discusses how Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks.
verdicts.evidence: The target page exists (it carries old /docs/guides/crosswalk/aws/ aliases), but it no longer mentions "Crosswalk" or "day one" tasks. It's just a list of guides: "This section contains guides for working with AWS services using Pulumi," covering the AWS, AWSx, EKS and other packages.
verdicts.framing_note: The blog describes the guide as explaining "how Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks," but the current page is an index of AWS package guides and never uses the Crosswalk branding.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Crosswalk for AWS" is legacy branding. The page only keeps crosswalk URLs as aliases, so the link text in the blog is probably out of date.

verdicts.text: Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) A Pulumi workshop called "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists. Its page says it "is designed to help new users become familiar with the core concepts needed to effectively deploy resources on AWS using Pulumi." Search indexes it at /events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/, not at the /resources/ path the claim cites. The /resources/ URL probably redirects through an alias, but I couldn't confirm that, and I also couldn't confirm the "on-demand" status.
verdicts.framing_note: The title and topic match. The canonical URL is /events/..., while the claim cites /resources/...
verdicts.intuition_flag: The cited /resources/ URL is not the indexed canonical path (/events/). Check content/events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws for an alias to /resources/..., or update the link.

verdicts.text: Users can sign up to try Pulumi at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
verdicts.evidence: Line 180 links "[try Pulumi](https://app.pulumi.com/signup)". The same signup URL shows up across many sibling pages and layouts: layouts/partials/cta-get-started.html uses `href: "https://app.pulumi.com/signup"`, and content/docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud.md says "[Sign up for a Pulumi account](https://app.pulumi.com/signup)".

verdicts.text: There is a blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ that covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: pulumi/docs PR #21651 adds the post at content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md with the title "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi." The PR says the post explains what "built on the Pulumi engine" means mechanically. I could not confirm that #21651 has merged, so the /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ link only resolves once it does.
verdicts.framing_note: The PR says the new post covers what "built on the Pulumi engine" means mechanically and leaves the migration story to the 2024 post. The claim's wording, "engine mechanics behind SST's migration", is close to this but frames the post around the migration.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link target is added by a companion PR (#21651). Check that it merges before or together with this PR, or the link will 404.

verdicts.text: SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's official docs say: "SST is a framework that makes it easy to build modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure." The claim is a light paraphrase of this tagline and keeps its meaning.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "makes it easy to build ... on your own infrastructure" and the claim says "makes building ... on your infrastructure easy". Only the word order changed, so the assertion is the same.

verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
verdicts.evidence: In the sst/ion repo, an earlier version of the README says: "SST v3 uses a new engine for deploying SST apps. It uses Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." The repo is named "ion", and the current README says it "was for work on sst v3". That supports "Ion" being the code name for the new Pulumi-based engine.
verdicts.framing_note: The README credits the engine to both Pulumi and Terraform (Terraform providers underneath). The claim only mentions Pulumi, which is a simplification, not an error.

verdicts.text: SST Ion's constructs (or components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
verdicts.evidence: SST's current platform (v3, the Ion line) lists "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0", "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0" and other Pulumi providers as its dependencies. It has no aws-cdk-lib or CloudFormation dependency, so its components deploy through Pulumi rather than CDK/CFN.
verdicts.framing_note: The dependency list is indirect evidence of the deployment engine, but it clearly supports the claim.

verdicts.text: SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own providers doc (sst/sst www/src/content/docs/docs/providers.mdx, decoded from base64) says "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and **supports 150+ providers**". It also links provider configuration to Pulumi Registry pages. Most of those Pulumi providers are Terraform providers bridged through Pulumi, so the claim holds, but the page never uses the word "bridge", which is why confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs (sst/sst providers.mdx) say "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and **supports 150+ providers**", and they point users to pulumi.com registry pages for AWS/Cloudflare provider inputs. That means SST's providers are Pulumi packages, including Terraform-bridged ones. I didn't find the exact wording "behind the scenes for the deployment engine" in SST's docs, so the deployment-engine part rests on indirect evidence.

verdicts.text: SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform, with potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs confirm the Console is a paid managed product: "Starting Feb 1, 2025, the Console will be priced based on the number of active resources in your SST apps," and it offers volume pricing if you contact them. No public source gives SST's revenue breakdown, so the claim that it "primarily relies" on SaaS revenue can't be checked. None of the results mention enterprise services or consulting income.
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/docs/console/; https://sst.dev/blog/console-pricing-update/; WebSearch ran query "SST console pricing business model revenue"
verdicts.intuition_flag: This reads like a hedged guess about how a private, VC-backed company makes money. The "enterprise services and consulting" part is speculation with no source. Consider rewording it as a factual statement that SST monetizes through its paid Console.

verdicts.text: The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: SST's official Console docs say: "The Console is completely optional and comes with a free tier." The current free tier covers workspaces with 350 active resources or fewer.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "completely optional and comes with a free tier" and the claim says "optional and includes a free tier", so they assert the same thing.

verdicts.evidence: This is the blog post's own front matter publication date (`date: 2026-09-16`). It is metadata the author sets, not a factual assertion that an outside source could check.

verdicts.text: SST v3 replaced AWS CDK with an embedded Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's v3 announcement says "SST was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation" and describes a new deployment engine "that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." Ion then shipped as v3. SST's post "Moving away from CDK" backs up the "embedded" part: you install only the SST CLI, and "There's nothing else to install."
verdicts.framing_note: The source says v3 replaced CDK and CloudFormation with Pulumi and bridged Terraform providers. The claim mentions only CDK and the Pulumi engine, which is a correct subset of that.

verdicts.text: SST v3 (the Ion-based rewrite) replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own v3 announcement says SST "was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation" and that Ion, now released as v3, is a new engine "that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation". It also says "There are no CDK constructs. Instead there is an AWS provider from Pulumi that's built on Terraform."
verdicts.framing_note: The source says Pulumi + Terraform (bridged) providers replaced CDK/CloudFormation, which matches the claim. "Embedded engine" is a fair paraphrase of SST bundling Pulumi. Not every SST provider is necessarily Terraform-bridged, but the AWS one is.

verdicts.text: SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post describes Ion (released as SST v3) and says that on `sst deploy`, resources "make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls". The SST v3 post also says the new engine uses "Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim matches SST's own description: embedded Pulumi engine → bridged Terraform provider → AWS SDK calls, replacing CDK and CloudFormation.

verdicts.text: Nitric and Defang run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
verdicts.evidence: Nitric docs: "Nitric uses the Pulumi Automation API for its pre-built Pulumi Providers," and direct-deployment providers "use Pulumi under the hood." Defang's pulumi-defang README says its CD program "translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs pulumi up (or destroy etc.)" to provision resources.
verdicts.framing_note: Nitric also offers Terraform providers that generate IaC, but its official direct-deployment providers are all Pulumi-based, so the claim holds for its standard deployment path.

verdicts.text: Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
verdicts.evidence: The fetched page (HTTP 200) is truncated to the repo title, "Defang Pulumi providers - Take your app from Docker Compose to a secure and scalable cloud deployment with Pulumi." The quoted phrase "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" does not appear in what was fetched.
verdicts.framing_note: The repo tagline supports the general idea of going from Compose to a Pulumi deployment, but it doesn't contain the verbatim quote the claim attributes to Defang.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim presents this as a direct quote, so check that the exact wording appears in the README or Defang's docs. The "translates to a Pulumi program and runs pulumi up" wording may describe the Defang CLI rather than the provider.

verdicts.text: The SST team has repeatedly described their own architecture, since the Ion rewrite shipped, as being built on an embedded Pulumi engine calling Terraform-bridged providers.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." The Ion announcement post on SST's blog says the same thing: "the Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers." Since SST describes this in more than one place, "repeatedly" is supported.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's sources say "Pulumi behind the scenes for ... the deployment engine" and "Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi". The claim says "embedded Pulumi engine calling Terraform-bridged providers". Same meaning; "embedded" is a small paraphrase of "behind the scenes".
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Since the Ion rewrite shipped" is only partly accurate: the Jan 2024 blog post was written before Ion shipped, while the current docs page is from after it shipped.

verdicts.text: SST's latest release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page (HTTP 200) is the OpenCode AI coding agent homepage. It says nothing about SST releases, v4.17.1, or July 2026; it describes "The open source AI coding agent" with "over 208,000 GitHub stars". The source this line binds to doesn't address the claim.
verdicts.framing_note: This link probably belongs to a nearby sentence about OpenCode rather than to the SST version claim. The SST GitHub releases page (github.com/sst/sst/releases) is the right place to check it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A version-and-date claim cited to an unrelated product homepage. The "latest release" wording will go stale, and the version and date should be checked against the SST GitHub releases.

verdicts.text: Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install.
verdicts.evidence: SST's source (pkg/global/pulumi.go, decoded) has `NeedsPulumi()`, which checks for a pinned `PULUMI_VERSION` binary in SST's own BinPath. `InstallPulumi()` then downloads it automatically from `https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/releases/download/...`, so users never install Pulumi themselves. One nuance: SST fetches the Pulumi CLI on demand rather than shipping it inside its binary, so the same line's wording "the engine ships inside the SST CLI" is a bit loose.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Sibling phrase "engine ships inside the SST CLI" is imprecise: SST downloads a pinned Pulumi CLI into its own bin dir on first use rather than bundling it.

verdicts.text: SST keeps deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say state is "stored in a file locally and backed up to a bucket in your AWS (or Cloudflare) account". The State page describes the bootstrap bucket "typically named sst-state-<hash>", created in the app's home region. The claim is right when AWS is the home. Cloudflare is also supported as a home, so the S3 location is the AWS case, not the only option.
verdicts.framing_note: The source covers either an AWS or a Cloudflare home. The claim describes only the AWS case, which is the default and the most common setup.

verdicts.text: The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine as described in this post.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own materials make this point more than once over time. The v3 launch post (Aug 2024) describes "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." SST's Providers docs (2026) state "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers."
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/blog/sst-v3/ ; https://sst.dev/docs/providers/ (WebSearch ran query "SST v3 Ion built on Pulumi Terraform providers")
verdicts.framing_note: SST's own sources say "built on Pulumi/Terraform" and "use Pulumi and Terraform". The claim's "repeatedly" rests on two first-party statements (2024 launch post, 2026 docs). "Embedded Pulumi engine" is the post's wording, not a quote from SST.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Repeatedly stated" is vague attribution. Consider citing the SST v3 post or providers doc directly.

verdicts.text: `sst deploy` handles the provisioning end to end.
verdicts.evidence: SST docs say "When you're ready to deploy your app, you can use the deploy command," and that components "create the necessary infrastructure in your AWS account." DeepWiki's write-up of sst deploy describes "the complete deployment pipeline from configuration building through Pulumi execution to state persistence."
verdicts.framing_note: "End to end" is the author's own loose wording. The sources back the idea that one sst deploy command builds the config, runs Pulumi, provisions the resources and saves state. The DeepWiki source is a secondary, auto-generated summary.

verdicts.text: SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
verdicts.evidence: The sst.dev homepage loaded (HTTP 200), but the part we got back never says "open source", "TypeScript framework", "Serverless Stack" or "150 providers". It only says "For whatever you build. Deploy everything your app needs with a single config." Its sample code does use non-AWS providers (planetscale, cloudflare).
verdicts.framing_note: The page we fetched doesn't contain the passage the claim relies on; the body was cut off after the hero section.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim bundles three separate facts (open source/TypeScript, former Serverless Stack name, 150+ providers). The '150 other providers' figure most needs checking against SST's docs, since the count would come from Pulumi/Terraform bridged providers.

verdicts.text: In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post "Moving away from CDK" (January 29, 2024) says "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications", deployed with Pulumi rather than CDK/CloudFormation. It also says "We decided to build a prototype a couple of months ago", which puts the start in late 2023.
verdicts.framing_note: "Late 2023" is worked out from "a couple of months ago" in a January 2024 post. "Entire deployment layer" matches replacing the CDK+CFN engine with Pulumi.

verdicts.text: SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."
verdicts.evidence: The fetched post's "What Is Ion?" section says, word for word: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi ; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." The post's title is "Moving away from CDK", as the claim states.
verdicts.framing_note: The quote is word-for-word. The only difference is spacing around 'Pulumi ;', which comes from how the page text was extracted.

verdicts.text: SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
verdicts.evidence: The cited page loaded (HTTP 200) and is the right post: "Moving away from CDK | SST ... Jay January 29, 2024." It also says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi," which fits the claim. But the fetched text cuts off before the "How Does Ion Work" section, so the exact sentence about `sst deploy` and the "embedded Pulumi engine" could not be found or quoted.
verdicts.framing_note: The quoted sentence is probably in the "How Does Ion Work" section, which is missing from the truncated fetch. The visible text fits the claim but does not confirm the exact wording.

verdicts.text: SST's docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
verdicts.evidence: The cited URL returned HTTP 200, and its title is "What is SST | SST", so the page name matches. The pre-fetched body cuts off in the navigation sidebar and does not include the quoted sentence about Pulumi, so I can't confirm the quote from what was fetched.
verdicts.framing_note: The supporting passage wasn't in the fetched part of the page, so no framing comparison was possible.

verdicts.text: That's confirmed outside SST's own writing, too. Independent developers who've compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture:
verdicts.evidence: Third-party comparison articles describe the same architecture. cdkbase (SST vs Terraform, 2026) says SST v3 "rebuilt on the Pulumi engine with Terraform providers underneath." Encore's comparison calls SST "a higher-level layer on top of Pulumi." Neither is SST's own writing.
verdicts.framing_note: This sentence introduces a quote that follows it. I couldn't see which article the post actually quotes, so I checked the general claim ("independent comparisons describe SST as built on Pulumi") and not that specific quote.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Encore and cdkbase are vendors with their own products to sell, not purely "independent developers." The quote that follows should be checked on its own.

verdicts.text: Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" states: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
verdicts.evidence: The page returned HTTP 200 and is Gautier Blandin's article, but the pre-fetched body cuts off in the Pulumi "Strengths" section, before the SST section. So I can't confirm the quoted sentence. The page title also differs from the claim: it reads "Terraform vs Pulumi vs SST A tradeoffs analysis", not "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis".
verdicts.framing_note: Couldn't find the quoted passage because the fetched body is truncated. Separately, the article title is quoted wrong: the page has "Terraform vs Pulumi vs SST / A tradeoffs analysis".

verdicts.text: Kiryl Anoshka's post "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" states: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
verdicts.evidence: The page returned 200 and confirms the title and author: "headline":"SST Ditches AWS CDK: Time to Move on to Ion", author "Kiryl Anoshka". The fetched body is cut off before the quoted sentence about Pulumi imports, so I couldn't check the quote itself.
verdicts.framing_note: Title and author attribution match. The quoted passage wasn't in the fetched text, which was truncated, so I couldn't check its wording.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The quote sounds like it's from this article (it discusses the imports of SST v2 constructs, then Ion), but a reviewer should check the exact wording against the full page.

verdicts.text: The `platform/package.json` in the `anomalyco/sst` repository (formerly `sst/sst`), verified September 2026, lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
verdicts.evidence: The fetched package.json `dependencies` block includes all eight packages: "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0", "@pulumi/cloudflare": "6.15.0", "@pulumi/command": "1.0.1", "@pulumi/docker-build": "0.0.14", "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0", "@pulumi/random": "4.16.6", "@pulumi/tls": "5.0.1", "@pulumiverse/vercel": "4.6.0".
verdicts.framing_note: All eight named packages are listed under "dependencies" (not devDependencies). The page doesn't show the "formerly sst/sst" rename or the "verified September 2026" date, so those parts weren't checked.

verdicts.text: The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more.
verdicts.evidence: sst/sst platform/package.json (@sst/platform) lists "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0", "@pulumi/cloudflare": "6.15.0", "@pulumi/docker-build": "0.0.14", plus @pulumi/command, @pulumi/random and @pulumi/tls. All of these are first-party pulumi/* providers. It also depends on @pulumiverse/vercel, which is a community provider, but the claim's "and more" doesn't depend on that one.
verdicts.framing_note: This checks the package.json in the repo source, not the tarball published to npm. The dependency list should be the same.

verdicts.text: In the SST/Pulumi deployment chain, `sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, which is SST's responsibility.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's docs say the run function in sst.config.ts is where "you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components." They also say SST's built-in components "Internally they use Pulumi's AWS provider." DeepWiki's write-up of sst/sst describes the CLI bundling sst.config.ts and injecting the `sst` global modules before handing the deployment to Pulumi. Together these support the claim that SST reads the config and resolves its own components.
verdicts.framing_note: No single page states the "SST's responsibility" split in those words. It follows from SST owning the config parsing and bundling plus the sst.* component library, with Pulumi running underneath as the engine.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi engine diffs desired state against actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi docs say "The deployment engine computes the set of operations needed to drive the current state of your infrastructure into the desired state expressed by your program." Ordering operations by resource dependencies is standard engine behavior. One caveat: the "current state" the engine compares against is the state Pulumi has stored, not live cloud state. The State docs say Pulumi skips an implicit refresh on every up/preview.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs say "current state"; the claim says "actual state". That's a loose paraphrase: without `pulumi refresh`, Pulumi compares against its recorded state, not the live infrastructure.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Actual state" may suggest Pulumi checks live cloud state on every update. "Last recorded state" or "current state" would be more accurate.

verdicts.text: In the SST architecture, state is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account, self-hosted rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's State docs say that when bootstrapping, SST creates "A bucket to store the state, typically named sst-state-<hash>. This is created in the region of your home." It also says "Your state file is uploaded to your home." A third-party write-up adds that SST "backs it up to your AWS account", so the state is self-hosted and not in Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.framing_note: SST lets the "home" be either aws or cloudflare. The claim covers the AWS case, where state goes to an sst-state S3 bucket in the user's account.

verdicts.text: Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, and this is handled by Pulumi's Terraform bridge.
verdicts.evidence: The fetched page confirms only that the repo is "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." It does not say the bridge turns resources into cloud API calls. In bridged providers, the upstream Terraform provider code makes the cloud API calls. The bridge connects Pulumi's provider protocol to that provider.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim — the source says 'library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi', but the claim says the bridge 'translates each resource into cloud API calls'.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine owns the provisioning mechanics underneath SST: dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi concepts docs say the "Deployment engine computes the set of operations needed to drive the current state of your infrastructure into the desired state expressed by your program", and resource properties "handle any necessary dependencies". SST's own docs, quoted in the post, say SST "uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine". One nuance: the providers make the actual cloud API calls and the engine orchestrates them, so "plumbing to provider APIs" is a loose way of putting it.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/iac/concepts/_index.md L44-58; SST docs quote at content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md L57
verdicts.framing_note: The claim describes Pulumi engine architecture in general terms. I couldn't check it against the pulumi/pulumi source because the GitHub search hit a rate limit.

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
verdicts.evidence: AWS says CloudFormation already supported "170+ AWS services spanning over 900 resource types" by April 2022, and a 2026 third-party catalog lists 1,613 CloudFormation resource types. The rhetorical point (a very large number of resource types, each with its own lifecycle) holds, but "hundreds" undersells the real count, which is now over a thousand.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Hundreds" understates it: AWS now has more than 1,600 CloudFormation resource types, so consider saying "well over a thousand".

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
verdicts.evidence: The state docs say Pulumi supports DIY backends as well as Pulumi Cloud: "a 'Do It Yourself' backend that stores state in an object store you manage—AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, ... or your local filesystem." With a DIY backend, the engine runs without a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud. Pulumi Cloud is only the default backend.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Pulumi-hosted service" is absolute: when a plugin isn't installed locally, the CLI may by default download provider plugins from Pulumi-hosted locations (e.g. get.pulumi.com). A reviewer may want to add a qualifier.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API works for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools the same way Pulumi's engine embeds without requiring a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: The Automation API docs say it "drives the Pulumi CLI under the hood". The state docs say the CLI can use a self-managed backend if you "Set the `PULUMI_BACKEND_URL` environment variable" or set `backend: url:` in Pulumi.yaml, both of which Automation API workspaces can pass through (project settings or environment variables). So embedding with Automation API doesn't require Pulumi Cloud, even though the step-by-step guide assumes a Pulumi Cloud access token.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim relies on self-managed backend support, which the docs describe for the CLI in general. Automation API runs on that same CLI, so the claim follows as a special case. The Automation API guide itself lists a Pulumi Cloud token as a prerequisite, which readers could find inconsistent.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Terraform bridge is built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing and maintaining their own providers.
verdicts.evidence: The cited repo describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That supports the core fact that Terraform providers get adapted for Pulumi. It doesn't say the bridge was built "specifically" for downstream projects like SST so they can avoid maintaining their own providers.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says 'a library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi', but the claim says it was 'built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem ... instead of writing and maintaining their own providers'. The claim adds a purpose aimed at downstream projects that the source never states.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The bridge mainly exists so Pulumi can publish its own bridged providers. SST benefits from that indirectly, so saying it was built 'specifically' for projects like SST probably overstates the intent.

verdicts.text: Nitric's own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
verdicts.evidence: The cited nitric.io homepage returned HTTP 200, but it doesn't contain the quoted sentence and doesn't mention Pulumi or deployment providers. The page now promotes Suga ("Suga is what came out of it: hosting for agents, apps, and platforms") and links to docs.suga.app, so the quote needs a more specific Nitric docs URL.
verdicts.framing_note: The link goes to the marketing homepage, not the docs page the quote is attributed to ("Nitric's own docs"), so no supporting passage was available to compare.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Nitric seems to have rebranded or pivoted to Suga. The quoted docs page may have moved or been archived, so the citation should point to the specific docs page or an archived copy.

verdicts.text: Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources that don't have a dedicated SST construct yet can still be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
verdicts.evidence: SST's config docs say the run function "is where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components," and SST states it "uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine." So Pulumi resources can be defined and deployed right next to SST components in the same app.
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs say resources can be defined 'using SST or Pulumi's components' in run(). That covers the claim's specific case: resources with no SST construct yet. SST v3 calls these 'components', not 'constructs'.

verdicts.text: SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's broadened public attention.
verdicts.evidence: SST's current default-branch platform/package.json still lists "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0" among its dependencies, along with @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare and other Pulumi providers. So the dependency on the Pulumi engine is still there, even with the team's added focus on opencode.
verdicts.framing_note: The causal part of the claim ("hasn't changed as a result of") is the author's reading. Source code can only show that the dependency still exists.

verdicts.text: If you already run SST, you are already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not you've written a line of Pulumi code yourself.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine," and it doesn't need a Pulumi account. This holds for SST v3 and later (Ion). SST v2 was "built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation," so the claim is only true for v3+ users.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim says 'if you already run SST' without a version. Legacy SST v2 apps (still in maintenance) use CDK/CloudFormation, not Pulumi. Consider adding 'v3 or later'.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's components feature allows sharing infrastructure patterns across a whole organization rather than just within one SST app.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's Components docs say "packages containing components become discoverable across the organization and can be consumed by any team" once they are published to the Private Registry. The Building & Extending guide also says Pulumi lets you "share infrastructure patterns across your organization."
verdicts.framing_note: The docs support org-wide sharing of components. The contrast with "one SST app" is the author's own framing, and the source doesn't cover it. Org-wide discovery through the Private Registry requires the Enterprise or Business Critical plan, but components can also be shared through Git repositories.

verdicts.text: Using Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, or components with an SST app does not require leaving the underlying Pulumi engine SST already uses.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own docs confirm the main fact: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine." They also say SST "only relies on the open-source parts of Pulumi" and "does not require a Pulumi account." No source found here shows that an SST app can plug directly into Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, or Pulumi components.
verdicts.framing_note: The source confirms that SST embeds the Pulumi engine. The claim's suggestion that Pulumi Cloud, policy, and components work with an SST app without extra migration is the author's own inference; no external source supports it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: SST stores state in its own S3/local backend and says no Pulumi account is needed, so using Pulumi Cloud may take real backend or config changes even though the engine stays the same. The sentence may understate how much work that is.

verdicts.text: Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: SST's v3 announcement (Aug 20, 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3" and that SST "was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation," with Ion being a new engine "that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." SST's earlier post says Ion components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: The August 20, 2024 GA date fits "mid-2024" as a loose description. The "embedded Pulumi engine" wording matches third-party descriptions saying only the SST CLI needs to be installed.

verdicts.text: SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's State docs say its bootstrap resources in your account include a "state bucket". A third-party write-up adds that SST "will provision an S3 bucket named like sst-state- in your AWS region and store the state JSON there", so SST does not use Pulumi Cloud for state.
verdicts.framing_note: SST can also keep state with Cloudflare (home: cloudflare, in R2), so "S3 in AWS" is accurate for AWS-home apps, which is the default.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI, and SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud, so users don't need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's docs say SST "does not require a Pulumi account and all the data about your app and its resources stay on your side." SST's v3 blog says state is "stored locally and backed up to S3 in your AWS account." A third-party write-up adds that because Pulumi is used only as an internal engine, "Only the SST CLI is installed."
verdicts.framing_note: Sources support no Pulumi account, state in the user's S3 bucket, and no separate Pulumi install. The claim leaves out that state is also kept locally ("stored locally and backed up to S3"). Nothing fetched confirms the specific mechanism "embedded directly in the SST CLI".
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Embedded directly" may be imprecise: the SST CLI may download or manage the Pulumi binary itself rather than compile the engine in. Worth checking in sst/sst source.

verdicts.text: Users do not need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's official docs say SST "does not require a Pulumi account and all the data about your app and its resources stay on your side." For the install half, a third-party SST v3 writeup says Pulumi runs only as an internal engine, so there is "no need to install both products individually. Only the SST CLI is installed."
verdicts.framing_note: SST's official docs support the no-account half. The no-separate-install half rests on a 2024 third-party blog plus SST docs showing that only the SST CLI is installed.

verdicts.text: SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." The SST v3 blog also says state "is stored locally and backed up to S3," which fits the claim that SST doesn't write Terraform state, though no source says outright that SST never invokes the Terraform CLI.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi" + Pulumi deployment engine. The claim's "no Terraform CLI / no Terraform state" part follows from how the bridge works (it uses Pulumi RPC to talk to the provider) and from SST's own state storage, but no source states it directly.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "SST's components are defined using Terraform providers" is too broad: SST also uses Pulumi-native providers that aren't bridged. Better wording would be "many of SST's providers are bridged Terraform providers."

verdicts.text: Because SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, users can define resources directly with Pulumi for anything that doesn't yet have a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
verdicts.evidence: SST's config reference says the run function "is where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi’s components", and SST docs note that "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine," so resources defined directly with Pulumi deploy in the same app.
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs say you can mix SST and Pulumi components in run(), and that Pulumi is the deployment engine. The claim's specific use case (Pulumi resources for anything SST has no component for) follows from that. The phrase "compile into Pulumi resource declarations" is loose wording for SST components being built on Pulumi, not a literal compile step.

verdicts.text: The blog post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, from SST's side.
verdicts.evidence: The linked post exists and is published (draft: false). Its title is "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi", and it says: "In this post, we’ll explore why SST moved to Pulumi, what challenges they overcame". It covers SST's early days on CDK and the limits of CDK and CloudFormation that pushed SST away.
verdicts.framing_note: Title and topic match. "From SST's side" is loose: Pulumi's Sara Huddleston wrote the post, though it tells the story from SST's point of view and embeds a video.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "From SST's side" could read as if SST wrote the post, but a Pulumi employee did.

verdicts.text: The doc page "How Pulumi IaC Works" covers the engine mechanics referenced throughout this post.
verdicts.evidence: The page exists at content/docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works.md with the title "How Pulumi IaC Works". It covers engine mechanics: "the language host, deployment engine, and resource providers, and how they interact when you run pulumi up."
verdicts.framing_note: The link target resolves and has the right title. The page covers the deployment engine, resource registration, state diffing, and resource operations.

verdicts.text: The blog post "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi" describes the bridge SST and others build on.
verdicts.evidence: The page at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ is live, and its title matches exactly: "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi". The post covers Pulumi's Terraform provider bridging ("At Pulumi, we've supported bridging Terraform providers for use in Pulumi from the b[eginning]"). The post itself doesn't mention SST, so the part about SST building on the bridge comes from the PR author, not the source.
verdicts.framing_note: The link target and title are correct, and the post covers the Terraform bridge. The source doesn't back the SST attribution, but it's incidental context, not something the link is cited for.

verdicts.text: The Automation API doc page describes how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does.
verdicts.evidence: The link resolves: content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md is at that path. The page describes embedding the engine in other tools: "so you can drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application instead of invoking the `pulumi` command from a shell", and it lists use cases such as "Building higher-level tools, such as custom CLIs over Pulumi". I could not confirm that SST itself uses Automation API: GitHub code search on anomalyco/sst was rate-limited (HTTP 429).
verdicts.framing_note: The page talks about embedding Pulumi in "your own application" and "higher-level tools" in general. The claim adds "the same way SST does", which assumes SST embeds Pulumi through Automation API. I couldn't check that part against SST's source.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "the same way SST does" is only right if SST's Go CLI embeds Pulumi via Automation API (sdk/v3/go/auto). I believe it does, but I haven't confirmed it.

verdicts.text: npm download stats for `sst` show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
verdicts.evidence: The cited URL is a rolling "last-week" endpoint. It now returns a different week, so it can't confirm or contradict the figure for Sep 5–11: {"downloads":1334575,"start":"2026-09-21","end":"2026-09-27","package":"sst"}. The claimed 796,291 for 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-11 is not in the fetched body.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source is a moving 'last-week' window (now Sep 21–27), but the claim pins a specific week (Sep 5–11). The author should cite the fixed-range endpoint instead: https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst
verdicts.intuition_flag: The citation can't be checked later because the rolling endpoint's value changes every week. A fixed date-range URL would stay reproducible.
